requirement: The application makes no network calls and imports no networking modules.
The core has no GUI, CLI or network imports.
Shipped dependencies are permissive or LGPL only; SBOM and licence report are produced per release.
The release check scans the shipped dependencies for known vulnerabilities; a scan that could not run is a failure, never a pass.
A self-contained package (Ubuntu, and from 1.2.0 Windows) runs without admin rights and without internet.
Builds are reproducible from pinned versions.
All UI strings live in one module.
IDs are safe as file names and on drawings; SI/AWG helpers.
Strict, immutable model; no coercion or unknown fields.
Referential integrity and duplicate IDs are checked on load, save and every transaction.
Human-readable, diffable, deterministic files; byte-identical round trip.
Corrupt files open in recovery mode; nothing is dropped silently.
Atomic saves, backups, plain-language disk errors.
Same project open twice is detected; on-disk change is detected.
Lossless migrations that keep the original files.
Model changes are transactions with consistent undo/redo.
Random edit/undo/save/reload sequences keep the model consistent.
The loader survives random and malformed input.
Starter library is clearly unverified example data with no invented numbers.
Rule configuration lives in files; standards numbers are placeholders.
`harness validate` / `check` / `migrate` with meaningful exit codes.
Design tokens meet WCAG 2.2 AA and category colours stay distinguishable under simulated colour blindness (dE >= 20).
The prototype supports the ten journeys, works offline and logs no console errors.
The committed prototype matches the generator and is self-contained.
The Qt editor supports the UX journeys (add units, connect safely, table and import, redundancy and findings, delete and undo, modes, search, files, recovery, read-only).
Diagram edits are validated operations that compose into transactions.
Units saved without positions get deterministic, non-overlapping ones.
Logical findings state what, why and how to fix; fixes are safe; waivers need a justification.
Imports show a per-row preview and apply as one undo step.
Autosave journal inside the project folder; restore after a crash.
The editor stays responsive at 200 units, 2,000 interfaces, 20,000 wires.
Regeneration of an unchanged project is byte-identical and produces an empty plan.
Generated harnesses keep stable IDs; released harnesses, locked wires and locked pins are never changed.
Sizing, mass and lengths never guess: missing inputs are listed.
An independent verifier detects missing, swapped, duplicated and outdated wiring.
Generating 2,000 interfaces and 20,000 wires takes under 10 s.
Generate shows a preview, applies as one undo step, shows status, the independent check and Explain.
Every design rule has a positive test (fires on a violation) and a negative test (quiet on a clean project).
Findings state what, why and how to fix; warnings are waivable with justification, errors are not; waivers persist and appear in the report.
A check that cannot run because of placeholders says so.
Design rules run in the background and never block edits; Show, Fix and Waive work from the Problems panel.
Every output type is produced from the model, deterministically (equal model, equal bytes), and carries the generator version and model hash.
Golden-file tests for every output type on three reference projects.
Drawings stay legible in greyscale: harness drawings draw wire colours on a dark outline and also write every colour as a code; system diagrams use dark colours plus dash patterns.
Stale and modified outputs are detected in the CLI and the editor.
Verifier v2 checks every artefact against the design; each check has a mutation test.
Outputs never invent numbers: undecided gauges, unknown lengths, masses and test limits are written as such.
Releasing needs a name and comment and is blocked by verifier or rule errors, stale plans or outputs, undecided gauges and unknown lengths; it writes a baseline and a change log entry.
Released harnesses, the interfaces they carry and the pins they use cannot be edited or deleted; a new revision unlocks and keeps the old baseline.
The diff of two baselines, or of the working design against a baseline, lists added, removed and changed objects exactly (property test).
A released harness that no longer matches its baseline is reported (rule and `harness check`).
Title blocks, change log table and revision report come from the data; the editor offers review, release, new revision, changes (marked on the diagram) and change log.
A release is blocked while a configuration file is marked as a placeholder, unless the releaser gives a written reason, which is kept in the change log and the baseline (D-135).
A release is blocked while the harness uses a part that is not approved or is example data, unless the releaser gives a written reason, which is kept in the change log and the baseline (D-136).
Every interactive control has an accessible name; text is at least 10 px at every UI scale; the canvas announces its content and the accessible alternative.
Random editing for thousands of steps keeps every invariant (integrity, rejected steps change nothing, save and load round trip, verifier clean after generation).
The user guide, rule reference and configuration reference are complete and in sync with the program.
Ubuntu packages: `.tar.gz` with install and uninstall scripts, and a reproducible `.deb` (the Windows packages are REQ-PKG-02).
The usability kit computes SUS and success correctly and prepares the task material.
Sizing arithmetic (AWG diameter and area, ampacity derating, voltage drop) agrees with exact arithmetic and with the defining points of the AWG scale.
Every tool requirement names the file that verifies it, and the traceability report is current.
The SDD has a component table (layer, purpose, dependencies) and a requirement-to-component trace, generated from the code and current.
Size, complexity and test metrics are collected by a tool.
Every delivery has a configuration file and SHA-256 values.
Every design rule names the standard requirements it serves; a rule can only cite a requirement that exists in `compliance/requirements`.
Standard value profiles are opt-in (`harness config --apply-profile`), cite the requirement each value comes from, fill only unset values, keep the placeholder flag, and invalid values are reported.

Rules from the supplied standards (connector and wire voltage, temperature margin, mating cycles, one manufacturer per connector pair, wire specification, power and return pins, bundle current) are silent until their numbers exist, say what they could not check, and cite their requirement IDs.
EMC wiring checks (shield bonding at both ends, one bundle per EMC class) are opt-in, and the EMC class appears on wire lists and labels only when classes are used; the output verifier checks it.
Pin allocation can leave an unassigned contact between power and return; without the setting nothing changes.
The mapping of the standard's family-group codes to the tool's part classes is recorded as a worksheet that states only what the supplied text says and cites existing requirements.
Every set of outputs includes `system/provenance.json` (tool version, model hash, library, settings with placeholder flags, design counts); the output verifier checks it against the design.
Messages about damaged project files give the file, and the line and column of the damage or the line of the set-aside object, and never quote file content.
source: UX/UI guidelines "error messages point to the exact line"

requirement: `harness schema FOLDER` writes JSON Schemas of the project files, made from the model, with an editor settings fragment; nothing is downloaded; the schemas cover every key the tool writes.
The editor offers File > New project from an example (blank, first-steps, minimal-satellite, small-satellite, flatsat), the same examples as `harness new`.
The Show filter in the Model tab bar shows one signal class, connector or bundle and fades the rest without changing the project; it stays on when the diagram changes and follows a new project.

A person can set the gauge, type, colour and length of one wire, and a label and a note; the first four lock the wire against generation, the last two are always kept, one undo step, a released harness refuses (D-161).

A field added after 1.3.0 is not written while it has its default value, so a project that does not use it keeps byte-identical files and outputs; the wire list shows Label and Note only when used (D-160).
A person can draw a wire between two pins of a harness, move its ends and delete it; generation keeps it as it is and says when it cannot (D-162).
Several wires may share a pin; the design rule `pin-shared` names the pin, and the verifier warns instead of failing when a drawn wire is among them (D-162).
A person can twist or shield selected wires together as a pair, quad, coax or overall shield; generation keeps the group (D-162).
A pin has a free-text function that the Devices tab edits, pasted blocks and the pinout import can fill, generation copies to the cable pin and the pinout tables list (D-163).
A person can give a connector and a harness a label that `labels.csv` prints; generation keeps it (D-163).
The pinout tables show the termination (crimp or solder) of the pins when any pin has one (D-163).

The Revisions area shows who made the last commit of the Git repository around the project folder, read from the repository files without starting Git, without a network and without keeping the e-mail address; a folder with no readable repository shows no line (D-164).

A person can save devices with their connectors and pinouts to a device library file and add them to another project; nothing in the project is replaced, a taken ID gets the next free one, and parts and interface types come with the device (D-165).
The parts import reads an export file of a parts program (InvenTree: CSV, TSV, JSON, XLSX) offline; the IPN is the part ID and the approval status is never guessed (D-165).

The interface takes every colour, type size and gap from one token source (`gui/theme/tokens.py`: light and dark themes, WCAG 2.2 AA contrast) and uses the bundled Inter and JetBrains Mono fonts; the font licences ship with the program; nothing is fetched.
The connector part picker shows what each part is (description, maker, pins, specification, approval, ratings) in the list tooltip and under the picker.

The parts library records its name, version, source and date (date entered by a person, YYYY-MM-DD, never read from a clock); `harness library` shows and sets them, `harness import-parts` records the file name and its SHA-256; provenance and the editor show them.
source: UX/UI guidelines "version, date and source visible"

requirement: A person can make an empty draft harness (New harness), add cable connectors from library parts with pins, and draw wires between them, with no interface behind it; generation never changes such a harness, and a project that does not use it keeps byte-identical files (D-166).
source: AIT feedback 2026-10 (create a project completely from scratch)

requirement: The Linux package checks for the libraries it cannot bring with it before it starts and says which one is missing and the `apt install` line that fixes it, instead of a traceback (D-167).
A release has four packages (the `.deb`, the `.tar.gz`, the Windows setup program and the Windows `.zip`) and one `SHA256SUMS`; nothing is built for macOS (D-149, D-168).
A blank project says where to start: the empty diagram has an Add a device button and a hint that names only controls that exist (1.6.0).
source: Owner question 2026-10-21 (create a blank project from scratch)

requirement: Every harness has a build workbook to build from: what is ready and what is open, a cut list in cut order, one block per connector, the parts, the labels and a test sheet with empty result columns; it has no formulas, is the same bytes for the same model and is checked cell by cell by the independent verifier; the PDF drawings are optional and a set with all or none of them is valid (D-169).

A person can set the strip length at each end of a wire, for one wire, a selection or every wire of a harness; Generate keeps it like a label and a note and reports a wire it cannot carry it over to; it does not lock the wire (D-170).

A pin can name the contact (a library part of category contact) the cable side uses; Generate copies it from the unit's pin to the cable connector's pin; the crimp tool is a field of the contact part; a release freezes these parts (D-170).

A harness can list accessories (sleeving, heat shrink, labels, backshells) with where they go, a length and a quantity; one whose connector or wire is gone is an integrity error; Generate keeps them or says which it could not keep; a released harness is locked with them (D-170).

The build data shows in the tables only where it is used (so a project that does not use it keeps its files), always in the build workbook with *to fill in* for what is missing, in the BOM as contact and accessory lines, and the independent verifier checks each of them (D-170).
